title: Assessing the gestural characteristics of non-human primate facial behaviors
short_title: Which gesture traits of primate facial behaviors predict the others, across species and social contexts?

abstract: Recent studies have begun to assess whether non-human primate facial behaviors can be produced gesturally, aiming to better understand the evolutionary roots of human language. Gestures are often characterized as intentional social behaviors that are utilized flexibly to influence the actions of others, ultimately serving to achieve specific social goals. Studies frequently use a checkbox system to evaluate the presence or absence of specific gestural characteristics that indicate social, intentional, flexible, and goal-oriented behavior. However, these approaches do not always consider that gesture characteristics can vary based on situational differences and social context, or that these characteristics may be interdependent. We assessed the predictive relationships between gestural characteristics of seven primate species, including chimpanzees, four species of hylobatids, and two species of platyrrhine monkeys. We coded the presence or absence of 10 gesture characteristics (inspired by the literature on great apes’ manual gesturing) across all observed facial behaviors. We also coded the social context in which each facial behavior was produced. We examined the predictive relationships between gesture characteristics within species and social contexts using Random Forests and average feature importance scores. We also generated similarity scores to assess the predictive importance of gesture characteristics across species and social contexts. Overall, we identified differences in the predictive relationships of gesture characteristics across species, with particularly notable variations in social contexts. We propose that further research is needed on the facial “gesturing” behaviors of other primate species, both captive and wild, to understand which physiological and psychological variables may contribute to these differences.

summary: Do non-human primates make facial gestures: facial movements that are aimed at someone and used flexibly to reach a social goal, as their hand gestures are? Studies usually tick a checklist of gesture characteristics, but these characteristics can depend on each other and on the social situation. This paper reanalyzes previously published video data on 1,651 facial behaviors from 45 captive primates of seven species (chimpanzees, four gibbon species, white-faced sakis and white-fronted marmosets), each coded for 10 yes/no gesture characteristics and one of 10 social contexts such as play, grooming or aggression. For every characteristic, random forests (with logistic regression as a check) predict it from the other nine, which shows how much information each characteristic carries about the others; cosine similarity then compares these profiles between species and between contexts. The profiles differ between species, and even more between social contexts, so claims about a species' facial gesturing should take the context into account.
key_findings: In chimpanzees, social directedness (recipient ID: the face is turned to one identifiable individual) and response waiting were the characteristics that best predicted the others; recipient ID had the highest average feature importance of any characteristic in chimpanzees (19.68). In the other species the top two differed, although recipient ID was in the top two for four of the six.

Mechanical ineffectiveness (the movement serves no biological or object-handling purpose) carried almost no information about the other characteristics: its average feature importance was 0.00 in six of the seven species and in seven of the nine analysed social contexts.

Across social contexts, response waiting while persisting had the highest average feature importance (median 13.99, range 10.22–16.83) and was among the top two predictors in five contexts: affiliation, agonism, food, grooming and play.
Species were more alike than social contexts: the similarity of gesture-characteristic profiles had a median of 11.03 across species and 10.10 across contexts, and it varied more across contexts.

High-arousal contexts (agonism, general arousal, play and sex) did not differ from the other contexts in average feature importance (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.88), and the logistic regression and random forest rankings broadly agreed (median Spearman correlation 0.74 across species).
